notes.meaning: Jephthah was a brave fighter who had a difficult start in life because his mother was a prostitute. Even with that painful family background, God gave him great courage and ability. God does not look down on people because of circumstances they could not control.

differ.view: Adam Clarke suggested that the word translated prostitute here originally meant an innkeeper or tavern hostess.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars view Gilead not as a personal father, but as a title for the clan or region added to the story later.

notes.meaning: Gilead's wife also had sons, and when they grew up, they drove Jephthah away from home. They told him he would receive no family inheritance because his mother was an outsider. Their harsh treatment showed personal hatred as well as a desire to keep the property for themselves.

Jephthah fled from his brothers and made his home in the land of Tob. Other poor and desperate men gathered around him, and he became the leader of their band. Like David living in the wilderness, Jephthah used his military skills to survive and fight against Israel's enemies.

Sometime later, the Ammonite army invaded Gilead and attacked Israel. The leaders of Gilead realized they had no general capable of facing this danger. They traveled to Tob to ask Jephthah to return and lead them.

The elders begged Jephthah to become their military commander so they could battle the Ammonites. Although they had pushed him out earlier, their extreme danger forced them to recognize his fighting skill. People who are rejected are often the very ones God uses in times of trouble.

Jephthah asked why the elders were coming to him now, since they had hated him and let him be expelled. The elders admitted their past wrong and offered to make him the ruler over all Gilead, not just a wartime general. Their great need led them to offer him full authority in exchange for his help.

Jephthah asked them plainly if they would truly keep him as their permanent head if the Lord gave him victory. The elders swore a solemn oath before the Lord, calling on God as their witness to keep their word. Jephthah wanted to be sure their promises were genuine before risking his life.

Jephthah went back with the elders, and the gathered people officially confirmed him as their ruler and general. Before taking any military action, Jephthah repeated his agreement before the Lord in Mizpah through prayer. He recognized that true authority and success depend entirely on God.

Jephthah sent messengers to the king of Ammon to ask why he had invaded Israel's land. The Ammonite king claimed that Israel had stolen the territory between the Arnon and Jabbok rivers when they left Egypt. Rather than rushing into war, Jephthah sought to settle the disagreement with truth and reason.

Jephthah sent envoys back to explain the true history of the land. He declared that Israel had never taken any territory from Moab or Ammon during their journey. Starting with the facts was his way of proving that Israel was completely innocent of the king's charges.

Jephthah reminded Ammon of how peacefully Israel had traveled through the wilderness. When the kings of Edom and Moab refused to let them pass through their lands, Israel patiently walked around them instead of attacking. They carefully stayed outside the borders of those nations to avoid causing any trouble.

Israel sent a polite request to King Sihon of the Amorites, asking only to pass peacefully through his land on their way home. Sihon refused to trust them, gathered his army at Jahaz, and attacked Israel without provocation. Israel fought only to defend itself against Sihon's hostile strike.

The Lord gave Israel complete victory over King Sihon and his army. Israel took possession of the Amorite lands from the Arnon to the Jabbok and from the desert to the Jordan River. Israel had taken this land from the Amorite invaders, not from the Ammonites.

Jephthah pointed out that the Lord God of Israel had driven out the Amorites to give the land to His people. Since God Himself had granted them the territory, Ammon had no moral or legal right to claim it. God's gifts and decisions stand firm against all outside complaints.

Jephthah challenged the Ammonites by arguing from their own point of view. He asked if they would not keep whatever territory their god Chemosh gave them, so Israel would certainly keep what the Lord had given. Jephthah used their own religious thinking to show that Israel's ownership of the land was completely fair.

Jephthah asked the king if he thought he was better than Balak, an ancient king of Moab who never tried to fight Israel over this territory. Israel had lived peacefully in Heshbon, Aroer, and nearby towns for three hundred years without any Ammonite claims. Three centuries of quiet possession proved that Ammon had no real right to the land.

Jephthah stated that Israel had done no wrong, but Ammon was sinning by starting an unjust war. He called on the Lord, the ultimate Judge, to decide between the two nations on the battlefield. The Ammonite king refused to listen to Jephthah's message, making the conflict unavoidable.

The Spirit of the Lord came upon Jephthah, giving him extraordinary courage and divine help to lead Israel. He traveled through Gilead and Manasseh to gather troops, then assembled his army at Mizpah to advance against Ammon. God provided the spiritual strength and wisdom Jephthah needed to do his work.

differ.view: Some Reformed commentators argue that because the Spirit came upon Jephthah here, his subsequent vow was made under the Spirit's guidance rather than in foolishness.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars view this verse as an editorial link connecting the earlier diplomatic messages to the war story.

notes.meaning: Before setting out to fight, Jephthah made a solemn promise to God. He vowed that if the Lord gave him victory, whatever came out of his house to meet him would belong to the Lord and be offered as a burnt offering. While he wanted to express thankfulness, his hasty vow showed a lack of trust and created an agonizing trap.

differ.view: Methodist commentators such as Adam Clarke believed Jephthah vowed either to dedicate a person to the Lord's service or sacrifice an animal, never intending human sacrifice.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic commentators teach that Jephthah made a reckless and mistaken vow that was tainted by surrounding pagan ideas of human sacrifice.

notes.meaning: Jephthah crossed over to battle the Ammonites, and the Lord handed them over to him. He struck down their forces and captured twenty cities, from Aroer all the way to Abel-keramim. This crushing defeat completely subdued the Ammonites and freed Israel from their oppression.

When Jephthah returned home to Mizpah, his daughter came out dancing and playing tambourines to celebrate his great triumph. She was his only child, and he had no other son or daughter to carry on his name. Her joyful welcome instantly turned his victory celebration into deep sorrow.

When Jephthah saw his daughter, he tore his clothes in extreme grief and cried out that she had brought him very low. He explained that he had made a solemn vow to the Lord and felt he could not take it back. His heart broke because his own thoughtless words now brought terrible sorrow to the one he loved most.

differ.view: Many Reformed teachers believe Jephthah should have broken his rash vow and repented, because keeping a vow that harms someone is worse than breaking it.

notes.meaning: Jephthah's daughter responded with remarkable courage and faith. She urged her father to keep his promise to God, since the Lord had granted complete victory over Israel's enemies. She placed God's honor and her father's integrity above her own comfort and future.

The daughter asked her father for two months to wander the mountains with her female friends so she could grieve that she would never marry. Jephthah agreed and sent her away for that time. In ancient Israel, dying without children or remaining unmarried was seen as a deep and painful loss.

After two months, she returned home to her father, and he carried out the vow he had made. The Bible notes that she never married, and her sacrifice led to a regular custom in Israel. Christian readers have long held different views on whether she was put to death on an altar or dedicated to lifelong celibacy at God's sanctuary.

differ.view: Methodist commentators argue that Jephthah dedicated his daughter to serve the Lord in lifelong virginity rather than killing her in violation of God's law.
Many Reformed commentators conclude that Jephthah literally sacrificed his daughter as a burnt offering in a tragic, misguided attempt to keep his vow.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic tradition generally teaches that Jephthah literally killed his daughter, influenced by pagan customs rather than God's commands.

notes.meaning: A lasting tradition grew in Israel where young women went out four days each year to remember and praise Jephthah's daughter. They commemorated her selfless spirit, obedience, and devotion to God. Her willingness to give up her future for her family and nation was remembered for generations.
